transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’m here because I’ve been having a hard time keeping my temper in check. I don’t mean to be difficult or scare anybody, but I keep snapping at people. There was this safety meeting at work, and I started yelling before I could stop myself. Now some of the younger inspectors seem nervous to ask me things, and… I don’t want to be that kind of person.
Do you often feel irritable or have outbursts even when things aren’t particularly stressful or frustrating?

I… I wouldn’t say all the time, but yes, it happens more than I’m comfortable admitting. I can be okay one minute and then I just snap, even if it’s not some huge thing. Like that safety meeting—I started yelling before I could really stop myself. I’m not proud of it. Now the younger inspectors seem afraid to ask me things, and that feels awful. I don’t want to come across like that.
When you feel yourself getting irritated or about to snap, do you also notice any physical restlessness, like needing to move around, pacing, or feeling on edge?

Yes… I think so. I try not to make a big deal of it, but even when I’m somewhere that should be fine—like the break room, or at rehearsal—I catch myself watching the doors, listening for sudden machine noises, checking if someone’s moving behind me. It’s like my body doesn’t quite believe I’m safe, if that makes sense.
Do you often feel like you're on high alert, as if you're constantly watching out for something to go wrong, or do you get easily startled by things like loud noises or someone surprising you?

Yes… I suppose I do. I try not to make it obvious, and maybe I’m making it sound worse than it is, but even in the break room or at rehearsal, I’m watching the doors, listening for sudden machine noises, noticing who’s moving behind me. It’s like my body just won’t quite believe I’m safe, even when I know I should be. Is that… the kind of thing you mean?
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things even when there's no immediate danger, or have trouble quieting your mind even when you want to relax?

Yes… I do have trouble shutting it off, I guess. I don’t mean to sound dramatic, but even when nothing’s happening—like in the break room, or at rehearsal—I’m still watching the doors, listening for machine noises, checking if someone’s behind me. I know, logically, I’m probably fine, but my body just doesn’t seem convinced. Is that what you mean?
Do you find yourself worrying about a variety of things — like work, relationships, or everyday responsibilities — even when there’s no clear reason to be concerned?

I’m not sure I’d say it’s a whole variety of things, no. I mean, I worry some—everybody does, right? Work and bills and keeping up with things—but I don’t know that it’s for no reason exactly. I guess I’m not sure how to separate normal worrying from… the other kind. Is that what you’re asking?
Do you find that your worrying happens more often than not, like most days you’re going over things in your mind even when you wish you could stop?

I don’t know if I’d say most days… maybe I’m not keeping track well enough. I do go over things in my head sometimes, but I guess I always thought that was just trying to be responsible, you know? I don’t want to overstate it. Maybe if you mean like constant worrying about everything, I’m not sure that fits. Does that make sense?
Have you noticed that you take less pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or that you feel down or hopeless more often than not?

I don’t think so… not more often than not, anyway. I mean, I have days where I’m not exactly cheerful, but I wouldn’t want to say I’m hopeless or anything like that if that’s not really fair. And I do still get some enjoyment out of things, I think. Maybe not always as much as I used to, but… I’m not sure. Does that answer it the right way?

Can you recall specific situations where your anger or irritability felt out of proportion to what was happening, and did these outbursts happen more than once in a short period of time, like several times in one week?

I… yes, I guess I can think of times. I don’t like saying “outbursts,” but there was a safety meeting where I started yelling before I could really stop myself. It felt like it came out bigger than the situation probably called for.

And it hasn’t been just once. I keep snapping at people at work, enough that some of the younger inspectors seem nervous to come ask me things now. I feel bad about that. I’m not trying to scare anybody.
Do you often feel physically restless or on edge even in places where you feel safe, like at home, or when you’re alone?

Yes… I mean, I try not to make a big thing of it, because I know I’m probably safe. But even in the break room, or at rehearsal, I catch myself watching the doors and listening for sudden machine noises. I’m checking who’s moving behind me before I even realize I’m doing it.

It’s like my head knows nothing’s happening, but my body doesn’t really believe it. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Can you think of a time recently when you felt genuinely happy or satisfied, even for a short while?

I’m trying to think… I mean, I’m sure there have been little moments. Maybe when something at work goes smoothly, or I get home and can just sit for a minute. I don’t know if I’d call it genuinely happy exactly, but satisfied, maybe briefly.

I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. It’s just… nothing big is coming to mind right away. Is that okay to say?
Have you noticed that your anger or irritability often happens even when nothing particularly frustrating or upsetting is going on, or does it usually feel like there’s a clear reason for it?

I think… there’s usually some reason, at least in my head. Like at work, if something feels unsafe or somebody isn’t listening, I can snap too fast. That safety meeting is the one I keep thinking about—I started yelling before I really had a chance to stop myself.

I don’t want to make it sound like I’m just angry all the time for no reason. But it does happen enough that people notice. Some of the younger inspectors seem scared to come ask me things now, and I hate that. I’m trying not to be that kind of person.
Do you find that you’re easily startled by things—like loud noises or someone suddenly appearing—and does it feel like you’re always waiting for something bad to happen?

Yes… I do get startled pretty easily. I try to tell myself it’s normal, like anybody would jump at a loud noise, but it feels stronger than that sometimes.

Even in the break room or at rehearsal, where I should know I’m okay, I’m still watching the doors, listening for sudden machine sounds, checking who’s moving behind me. It’s like I’m not trying to expect something bad, exactly… but my body is already waiting for it before I can talk myself out of it.

I don’t know if that answers it right.
Have you noticed that you feel fatigued or low on energy, even after getting enough rest?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I do get some sleep some nights, so I don’t want to overstate it, but it doesn’t feel very restful.

Most nights I’m either lying there until it’s almost morning before I can fall asleep, or I jerk awake from dreams where I hear the line alarms and that awful metal sound. Then even if I’ve gotten a few hours, I wake up feeling like I never really slept. So yes, I guess the low energy is there a lot. Is that the kind of thing you mean?

Do you find that you're constantly scanning your environment for potential threats, even in places you know are safe, and does this feeling interfere with your ability to relax or focus on what you're doing?

Yes… I think that’s a fair way to put it. I try not to make a big deal of it, because I know the break room or rehearsal aren’t dangerous places, but I’m still watching the doors, listening for sudden machine noises, and checking who’s moving behind me.

It’s like my head knows I’m okay, but my body doesn’t really believe it. And yes, it does make it harder to relax or stay focused. I can still do what I’m supposed to do, mostly, but part of me is always… somewhere else, keeping track. Does that make sense?
How long have you been feeling this way, where you’re constantly on edge and scanning your environment, even in places you know are safe?

It’s been… a while. Since the machinery accident, really—the one after they changed us to that overnight schedule.

I kept thinking it would settle down once some time passed, and maybe I told myself it had to be getting better, but if I’m being honest, it’s been about two years and four months now. That sounds like a long time when I say it out loud. Is that the kind of timeframe you’re asking for?

F06.3 (Anxiety not otherwise specified) remains as a possible residual category if full criteria for F43.1 are not met.
